To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cellulose nitrate membranes containing 10 wt% polyethylene glycol exhibit high permeability and selectivity for CO2 over O2 and N2.
the cellulose nitrate (CN)/polyethylene glycol (PEG) blend membranes show a selective permeation of CO2.
the permeability and the permselectivity of carbon dioxide increase with increasing fraction of polyethylene-glycol in the blend membrane.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of membranes with high selectivity and permeability for CO2.
the preparation of membranes which are selective for CO2 and which are useful for separation and concentration purposes.
the development of a new class of membranes that exhibit a high degree of CO2/N2 permselectivity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the permeation of CO2 through the cellulose nitrate film is governed by its plasticizing action.
the membrane is a selective permeation of carbon dioxide through a cellulose nitrate film.
the cellulose nitrate film containing 20 wt% polyethylene glycol is a selective membrane for CO2, which is suitable for practical use.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the permeability for gases is a function of both the free volume of the film and the interaction of the gas molecule with the film.

the cellulose nitrate films with a low content of polyethylene glycal were permeable to N2, O, and CO2, and the cellulose nitrafe films with a high content of polyethylene gylcol were selective for CO2.
cellulose nitrate is a suitable polymer for gas separations and the permeability and selectivity can be enhanced by adding a plasticizer such as polyethylene glycol to the cellulose nitrate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cellulose nitrate is a promising membrane for CO2 separation.
the cellulose nitrate membrane is a good membrane material for gas separation.
the permeability of CO2 through celluloses nitrate/polyethyleneglycol membranes can be controlled by varying the composition of the film.
